message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"2316e2c80929ae5ab6086a8e4c76eec42968e95842907f9c8aeef9a263d15d65","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:81","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","units":[{"unit_id":"sec01-u01","module_id":"sec01-m01","objective_ids":["sec01-u01"],"title":{"text":"Reading the license chart","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The license chart uses letters for classes and endorsements, and two letters mean different things depending on where they appear.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]},{"text":"Knowing which class fits which vehicle tells you which license and tests you need.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F18"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Alex holds a Class B commercial license and just bought a motorcycle.","fact_ids":["sec01-F19"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A commercial Class A, B or C license already covers Class D vehicles, but motorcycles always need Class M added.","fact_ids":["sec01-F19","sec01-F02"]},"result":{"text":"Alex adds Class M to the commercial license, as in Class AM, and needs no separate Class D.","fact_ids":["sec01-F19"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking Class H and the H endorsement mean the same thing.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"Class H is the hardship license for young drivers, while the H endorsement covers hazardous materials.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Class letters name the license; endorsement letters name the extra vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A chart shows the letter P. What two different things could it mean?","fact_ids":["sec01-R02","sec01-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"As a class, P is an instructional permit; as an endorsement, P covers vehicles seating sixteen or more.","fact_ids":["sec01-R02","sec01-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"The same letter does double duty, so check whether it is a class or an endorsement.","fact_ids":["sec01-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Your license chart","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Classes name the main license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"Endorsements add specific vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every Tennessee license carries a class, and some carry endorsements too. In this lesson you will learn what the main classes on the license chart mean, which endorsements exist, and where the commercial license takes over. Class D is the license for ordinary passenger vehicles that are not used for commercial purposes, other than vehicles in Classes A, B, C or M. Class M covers motorcycles and motor-driven cycles. Class P is an instructional permit, and Class H is a hardship license for young drivers. By the end you will be able to read the chart and spot the letters that trip people up.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The core classes","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class D: ordinary non-commercial passenger vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"Class M: motorcycles and motor-driven cycles.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"Class P: instructional permit issued with another class.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"Class H: hardship license for ages fourteen to sixteen.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the four classes most new drivers meet. Class D covers ordinary passenger vehicles that are not used for commercial purposes. Class M covers motorcycles and motor-driven cycles, and it can be issued on its own or alongside another primary class on the same card. Class P is an instructional permit, and it is issued together with a Class A, B, C, D or M license. Class H is a hardship license for drivers aged fourteen to sixteen who face special hardship. Each of these is a class, which means it names the main kind of driving the card allows.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-R06","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Endorsements add vehicles","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R03","sec01-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"F endorsement: driving for hire in a Class D vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R03","sec01-R04"]},{"text":"N covers large tanks; X adds hazardous materials.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R03","sec01-R04"]},{"text":"T covers double and triple trailers; S covers school buses.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R03","sec01-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Endorsements sit on top of a class and cover a specific kind of vehicle or work. The F, or For Hire, endorsement applies when a Class D vehicle is driven by someone employed mainly to drive it as a carrier of people or property. Several endorsements belong to commercial driving. The N endorsement covers tanks holding one thousand gallons or more, and the X endorsement combines tanks with hazardous materials. The T endorsement covers double and triple trailers, and the S endorsement covers school buses. When you read a license, the class comes first and the endorsements describe the extras.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R03","sec01-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Same letter, two meanings","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class H: hardship license for young drivers.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"H endorsement: hazardous materials.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"Class P: instructional permit.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},{"text":"P endorsement: vehicles seating sixteen or more.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two letters on the chart do double duty, and this is where many learners slip. The letter H can mean Class H, which is the hardship license for young drivers, or the H endorsement, which covers hazardous materials. The letter P can mean Class P, which is an instructional permit, or the P endorsement, which covers vehicles designed to seat sixteen or more people including the driver. So when you see H or P, ask yourself whether it is written as a class or as an endorsement. The class tells you what kind of license it is, while the endorsement tells you what extra vehicle the driver may handle.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01","sec01-R02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Motorcycles and off-road vehicles","fact_ids":["sec01-F16","sec01-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Over one hundred twenty-five cc: Class M.","fact_ids":["sec01-F16","sec01-F17"]},{"text":"Under one hundred twenty-five cc: Class M limited.","fact_ids":["sec01-F16","sec01-F17"]},{"text":"ATVs cross roads only at a right angle.","fact_ids":["sec01-F16","sec01-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Motorcycles are sorted by engine size. A motorcycle above one hundred twenty-five cubic centimeters calls for a Class M license, while one below one hundred twenty-five cubic centimeters calls for a Class M limited license. Off-road vehicles and ATVs follow stricter rules. They cannot be used for the road test, they may not be driven on Tennessee or federal highways, and they may cross a roadway only at a ninety-degree angle. Put simply, an ATV may cross a road straight across, but it may never travel along a highway, and it is never the vehicle for your driving test.","fact_ids":["sec01-F16","sec01-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick chart check","fact_ids":["sec01-R02","sec01-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"What two things can the letter P mean?","fact_ids":["sec01-R02","sec01-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: suppose a license chart shows the letter P, and a friend asks what it means. There are two possible answers, and both are on the Tennessee chart. Work it out before reading on. As a class, P is an instructional permit, issued together with a Class A, B, C, D or M license. As an endorsement, P covers vehicles designed to seat sixteen or more people including the driver. The lesson is that one letter can do double duty, so always check whether the letter is listed as a class or as an endorsement before you decide what it allows.","fact_ids":["sec01-R02","sec01-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Where commercial begins","fact_ids":["sec01-F18","sec01-F19","sec01-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Twenty-six thousand one pounds or more needs a CDL.","fact_ids":["sec01-F18","sec01-F19","sec01-F02"]},{"text":"A CDL covers Class D, but motorcycles still need Class M.","fact_ids":["sec01-F18","sec01-F19","sec01-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, remember where the commercial license takes over. Vehicles weighing twenty-six thousand one pounds or more require a Commercial Driver License in Class A, B or C. A valid commercial Class A, B or C license also covers Class D vehicles, so no separate Class D is needed. Riding a motorcycle, however, still requires adding Class M, written as a combination such as Class AM. Keep the core classes, the endorsements and the double meanings of H and P in mind, because the next lessons build on them as we look closely at Class D and the For-Hire endorsement.","fact_ids":["sec01-F18","sec01-F19","sec01-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec01-u02","module_id":"sec01-m02","objective_ids":["sec01-u02"],"title":{"text":"Class D and For-Hire","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F08"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Every resident driver needs the right license, and newcomers have a deadline to switch.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},{"text":"The For-Hire endorsement decides whether people who drive for work need extra testing.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Priya drives a shuttle as her full-time job in a Class D van that seats eight.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Her main job is carrying people in a Class D vehicle, so the For-Hire endorsement applies to her.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F05"]},"result":{"text":"Priya must add the For-Hire endorsement to her license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking any vehicle under the Class D weight limit can be driven on a Class D license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09"]},"correction":{"text":"A vehicle under twenty-six thousand pounds still needs Class C if it hauls hazardous materials, carries sixteen or more people counting the driver, or serves as a school bus.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"If driving is the job, add For-Hire; if driving helps the job, you usually do not.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A plumber drives a company van between job sites. Does the plumber need the For-Hire endorsement?","fact_ids":["sec01-F12"]},"answer":{"text":"Generally no, because the plumber drives only in the course of another job, though the employer may still require it.","fact_ids":["sec01-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"For-Hire is for drivers whose main job is carrying people or property.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who needs Class D","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every resident driver needs a license or TDL.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},{"text":"Newcomers must switch on a deadline.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers who must hold a Tennessee license, what Class D allows, and when drivers need the For-Hire endorsement. Every Tennessee resident who drives a motor vehicle needs either a valid Tennessee driver license or a Temporary Driver License, called a TDL. If you arrive with a valid license from another state or country, you must apply for a Tennessee license or TDL after living in Tennessee more than thirty days, upon working in Tennessee, or once you would qualify as a registered Tennessee voter. Any one of those three events starts the requirement to switch.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What Class D allows","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Up to twenty-six thousand pounds.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F10"]},{"text":"Age sixteen or older.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F10"]},{"text":"Vision, knowledge and driving tests.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"A Class D license lets you drive any vehicle weighing up to twenty-six thousand pounds at most. To get one you must be at least sixteen and pass three things: a vision screening, a knowledge test and a driving test. Anyone under eighteen must also meet the Intermediate Class D rules, which you will study in the graduated license lessons. So the Class D picture is simple to state: an age floor of sixteen, a weight ceiling of twenty-six thousand pounds, and three tests that every applicant must pass before driving alone.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Light but still Class C","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Hauls hazardous materials.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]},{"text":"Carries sixteen or more, counting the driver.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]},{"text":"Serves as a school bus.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people assume that any vehicle under the Class D weight limit can be driven on a Class D license. That is not true. A vehicle under twenty-six thousand pounds still needs a Class C license, not Class D, in three situations. The first is when it hauls hazardous materials. The second is when it carries sixteen or more people, counting the driver. The third is when it serves as a school bus. So weight is only part of the question; what the vehicle carries and how it is used can move it out of Class D entirely.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When For-Hire applies","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Main job is carrying people or property.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"Taxi, shuttle, ambulance drivers and couriers.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"Incidental job drivers usually exempt.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"The For-Hire endorsement is about why you drive. Drivers whose main job is carrying people or property in a Class D vehicle, such as taxi, shuttle or ambulance drivers and couriers, must add a For-Hire endorsement. People who drive only in the course of another job, such as plumbers, meter readers and engineers, generally do not need it, although an employer may still require it. The manual describes this endorsement as a bridge between the regular license for private travel and the commercial license needed for tractor-trailers, large trucks and buses.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Getting the endorsement","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Fee of four dollars and fifty cents.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]},{"text":"Two years of unrestricted Class D experience.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]},{"text":"Age eighteen, or sixteen for family business deliveries.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]},{"text":"Vision screening plus a Section B test.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Adding the For-Hire endorsement costs four dollars and fifty cents and requires two years of unrestricted driving experience in a Class D vehicle. Applicants must be at least eighteen, or sixteen when the vehicle belongs to their family business and is used only for that business's deliveries. For-Hire applicants also take a vision screening plus a separate knowledge test built from Section B of the manual. So the endorsement asks for a small fee, real driving experience, a minimum age and two tests, which together set it apart from an ordinary Class D license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"For-Hire check","fact_ids":["sec01-F12","sec01-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Does a plumber driving between jobs need For-Hire?","fact_ids":["sec01-F12","sec01-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a plumber drives a company van between job sites all day, but the job itself is plumbing. Does the plumber need the For-Hire endorsement? Work it out before reading on. Generally the answer is no. People who drive only in the course of another job, such as plumbers, meter readers and engineers, usually do not need the endorsement, although an employer may still require it. Compare that with a taxi or shuttle driver, whose main job is carrying people, and who must add For-Hire. The test is whether driving is the job or simply part of it.","fact_ids":["sec01-F12","sec01-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Class D in one view","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F09","sec01-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"License or TDL for every resident driver.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F09","sec01-F11"]},{"text":"Class C for hazmat, sixteen riders or school buses.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F09","sec01-F11"]},{"text":"For-Hire when driving is the job.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F09","sec01-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, every Tennessee resident who drives needs a valid Tennessee license or a TDL, and newcomers must switch after more than thirty days of residence, upon working here, or once they could register to vote. Class D covers vehicles up to twenty-six thousand pounds, but hazardous materials, sixteen or more people, or school bus use calls for Class C. If carrying people or property is your main job, you add the For-Hire endorsement, with its fee, experience, age and test requirements. Next, you will see how young drivers move from a learner permit toward Class D.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-F09","sec01-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec01-u03","module_id":"sec01-m03","objective_ids":["sec01-u03"],"title":{"text":"Permits and hardship licenses","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-F21","sec01-F22"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The Class PD permit is the usual first step toward Class D, with its own age and companion rules.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-F21"]},{"text":"The Class H hardship license is a rare exception with tight limits and a fixed end date.","fact_ids":["sec01-R07","sec01-F27","sec01-F29"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Jamal, fifteen, has just passed the Class D knowledge test and vision screening and received his Class PD.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A PD holder may drive only with a licensed driver who is at least twenty-one and sits in the seat beside him.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"result":{"text":"Jamal may practice only with a licensed adult of twenty-one or older seated next to him.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a hardship license lasts a year from approval.","fact_ids":["sec01-F29"]},"correction":{"text":"Every hardship license expires on the holder's sixteenth birthday, whatever age they were when approved.","fact_ids":["sec01-F29"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Permit at fifteen, adult of twenty-one beside you; hardship ends at sixteen.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-F21","sec01-F29"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Who may supervise a Class PD holder, and where must that person sit?","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"answer":{"text":"A licensed driver who is at least twenty-one, sitting in the seat beside the PD holder.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"rationale":{"text":"The companion rule names both an age and a seat, so a licensed adult in the back seat does not count.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"First steps to driving","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class PD: the learner permit.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-R07"]},{"text":"Class H: the rare hardship license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Most young drivers begin with a Class PD learner permit, and a very small number receive a Class H hardship license. This lesson explains both. A Class PD learner permit requires being at least fifteen and passing the Class D written knowledge test and the vision screening. The hardship license is far less common: fewer than one percent of the licenses issued to minors are Class H. You will learn the permit's companion rule, how a permit becomes a Class D license, and the strict limits that come with a hardship license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F20","sec01-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Driving on a PD","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"lines":[{"text":"Companion: licensed, at least twenty-one.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},{"text":"Companion sits in the seat beside you.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]}],"narration":{"text":"A Class PD holder may drive only with a licensed driver who is at least twenty-one and who sits in the seat beside them. Both parts of that rule matter. The companion must hold a license and be twenty-one or older, and the companion must be in the seat next to the permit holder, not somewhere else in the car. This is the core safety rule of the learner permit, and it applies every time the permit holder takes the wheel. A permit is a license to learn under supervision, not a license to drive alone. Keep that picture in mind for every practice drive.","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"From PD to Class D","fact_ids":["sec01-F22","sec01-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Road skills test required.","fact_ids":["sec01-F22","sec01-F23"]},{"text":"Under eighteen: hold the PD one hundred eighty days.","fact_ids":["sec01-F22","sec01-F23"]},{"text":"Knowledge test skipped unless permit long expired.","fact_ids":["sec01-F22","sec01-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Trading a Class PD for a Class D requires a road skills test, and drivers under eighteen must first have held the PD for one hundred eighty days under the Graduated Driver License law. A PD holder moving up to an Intermediate Class D skips the knowledge test, unless the permit expired more than twelve months before the driving skills test. So the usual path is simple: hold the permit for the required time, practice with your licensed companion, then pass the road skills test. Only a permit that lapsed for more than twelve months sends you back to the knowledge test.","fact_ids":["sec01-F22","sec01-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The hardship license","fact_ids":["sec01-F24","sec01-F25","sec01-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"Can be issued at fourteen.","fact_ids":["sec01-F24","sec01-F25","sec01-F26"]},{"text":"Family hardship and limited needs only.","fact_ids":["sec01-F24","sec01-F25","sec01-F26"]},{"text":"Proof mailed to the Driver Services Administrative Office.","fact_ids":["sec01-F24","sec01-F25","sec01-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"A Class H hardship license can be issued to a fourteen-year-old for a Class D vehicle, a Class M motorcycle or both, but only for family hardship and limited needs. The applicant mails proof of hardship with the application to the Driver Services Administrative Office, and approval brings a letter authorizing the application. The applicant must then pass vision, knowledge and road tests for a Class D vehicle, and adds the Class M knowledge and driving tests to ride a motorcycle, which is then limited to one hundred twenty-five cc.","fact_ids":["sec01-F24","sec01-F25","sec01-F26"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Hardship limits and end date","fact_ids":["sec01-F27","sec01-F29","sec01-F28"]},"lines":[{"text":"Daylight only.","fact_ids":["sec01-F27","sec01-F29","sec01-F28"]},{"text":"Only to places named in the letter.","fact_ids":["sec01-F27","sec01-F29","sec01-F28"]},{"text":"Expires on the sixteenth birthday.","fact_ids":["sec01-F27","sec01-F29","sec01-F28"]}],"narration":{"text":"The trap with hardship licenses is assuming they work like a normal license for a set period. A Class H license is good only during daylight and only for trips to the places named in the approval letter. Every hardship license expires on the holder's sixteenth birthday, whatever age they were when approved. A holder who is at least fifteen gets the same privileges as a Class PD holder when riding with one of the adults allowed for PD drivers. So the hardship license is narrow in time, narrow in place, and always ends on the sixteenth birthday.","fact_ids":["sec01-F27","sec01-F29","sec01-F28"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Permit companion check","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]},"lines":[{"text":"Who may supervise a PD holder, and from where?","fact_ids":["sec01-F21"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a Class PD holder wants to practice driving. Who may supervise, and where must that person sit? Work it out before reading on. The rule has two parts. The companion must be a licensed driver who is at least twenty-one, and that person must sit in the seat beside the permit holder. A licensed nineteen-year-old does not meet the age rule, and a qualifying adult riding in the back seat does not meet the seat rule.
